channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Why AI has no taste and how to fix it (w/ Thais Castello Branco) | E2319
gist: The founder of Taste Labs argues frontier models are trained to find the most-likely answer, which makes them structurally incapable of taste in subjective domains, and describes a two-sided business selling evals/preference data to frontier labs and opinionated 'taste' APIs plus a curated design index to app-layer companies, staffed by ~1,000 paid human 'tastemakers'. The news block dissects the collapse of Leopold Aschenbrenner's ~$45B AI-infrastructure fund (439% net return, ~4x leverage, margin-called, public book sold to Citadel while ~$5B of Anthropic stock is retained), the emerging platform-level war on AI slop (LinkedIn, Substack/Pangram, Google Earth + Nano Banana), and self-driving's commoditization colliding with driver-job politics in the US and China.

themes.theme: Why LLMs regress to the mean

insights.claim: Taste Labs' founder attributes AI's design/writing weakness to the training objective itself: models are optimized to produce the most likely correct answer, which works for math and code but is the wrong target in subjective domains where excellence is out-of-distribution.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: Implies taste cannot be fixed by scaling the same pretraining/RLHF recipe — it needs a separate preference-data layer, which is exactly the wedge Taste Labs is selling to the labs.
insights.quote: you have models that can solve cyber hack can solve PhD level math problems and they can't like write a good tweet or make a good design

insights.claim: The specific failure mode is averageness, not incoherence: model output looks like the mean of its training data, which is by construction the thing a viewer does not look at twice.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: Reframes 'AI slop' as a distributional problem with a measurable target (variety/out-of-distribution quality), which is what makes it benchmarkable and therefore sellable.
insights.quote: The average is that thing that you're going to kind of not even take a second glance at that you've seen a lot.

insights.claim: A second, distinct defect is collapse of personalization: two users prompting for completely different things get near-identical outputs, meaning models fail to fit the prompt and user intent, not just fail on aesthetics.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: Two separable product opportunities: raising the floor on craft quality, and intent/style fit — the latter is closer to a defensible personalization moat.
insights.quote: both of you could, for example, prompt to for two completely different things, but then the end output would like look the same

insights.claim: Calacanis generalizes the mechanism beyond AI: aggregating everything rather than skimming the cream guarantees regression to the mean, so any system trained on all available design, tweets, and blog posts will output average work.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Argues data curation — not data volume — is the binding constraint in subjective domains, favoring companies that own or license curated corpora over those scraping at scale.
insights.quote: In fact, when you take everything, you're guaranteed to have regression to the mean.

insights.claim: Taste Labs is sequencing the problem as quality first, personalization second, on the view that current model output quality is so low that style-fit is a premature optimization.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: Signals the near-term product is benchmark/eval and floor-raising work, and that a personalization product is a later-stage expansion — relevant for how to underwrite the company's roadmap.
insights.quote: because part of it right now is the bars are still on the ground and the first job is just let's lift the bar off the ground

insights.claim: The taste gap includes foundational perception failures, not only aesthetics: Taste Labs finds frontier models breaking on vision and 2D reasoning, which sit beneath any higher-order judgment about creativity or style.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: Suggests a concrete, testable capability gap in multimodal models that a specialist eval vendor can monetize with the labs today rather than waiting on subjective taste.

insights.claim: Both hosts converge on comedy and Twitter-native writing as the domains where LLMs are most visibly failing, with Grok cited as marginally better at platform idiom but still not funny enough to publish.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris (co-host) and Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Marks the next likely expansion market for taste/preference-data vendors after visual design, and a persistent gap consumer AI products cannot yet ship into.
insights.quote: Claude isn't funny. Claude's many things.

themes.theme: Taste Labs' two-sided model: labs plus app layer

insights.claim: Taste Labs runs two businesses at once: benchmarking and evaluating frontier models for the labs, and shipping opinionated tools/APIs for application-layer and agent companies that never touch the model weights.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: The infra/API half is the higher-multiple, non-services piece — worth watching whether revenue concentration stays in lab-funded data work or shifts to product.
insights.quote: half of our business maybe looks more like that like half is more like data our environments uh but the other half is is tools it's API

insights.claim: Taste Labs deliberately resists being categorized as a data-labeling/annotation vendor like micro1, positioning itself as data plus environments plus infrastructure — a distinction the founder credits to coming from an infra background before founding the company.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: Category matters for valuation: annotation shops are priced as services, agent-infrastructure companies as software — the pitch is explicitly an escape from labeling comps.

insights.claim: For app-layer customers who cannot change the model, Taste Labs' answer is to improve the generation before it starts by injecting the right context, on the premise that most users of Lovable, Cursor, Codex, Claude, or Figma are not professional designers and cannot express what they want in the correct terminology.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: Identifies a context-injection middleware layer sitting between vibe-coding tools and their non-expert users — a plausible acquisition target for those same tools.

insights.claim: Taste Labs is building a proprietary design index plus a judgment system that verifies whether an output stays on brand, both assembled from expert human curation rather than scraped data.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: On-brand verification is the enterprise wedge — it is the compliance-shaped problem marketing teams will pay for once they generate assets at volume.

insights.claim: The data Taste Labs collects is not just ratings: it includes senior-designer-style written critiques explaining why work is good or bad, curated good/bad exemplar pairs with reasoning, and from-scratch expert versions of what a perfect output would look like versus the LLM attempt.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: A taxonomy of the data shapes labs are actually buying for subjective domains — useful for evaluating any competitor claiming to sell 'taste data'.

insights.claim: Taste Labs raised an $18.5M seed round co-led by CRV and Amplify, is based in San Francisco and strongly in-person, and is hiring across engineering, research, operations, and a novel 'design researcher' role that studies what 'good' means as a field of study.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris (co-host) and Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: Concrete financing and burn signal for a pre-product-maturity data/infra startup, plus evidence that a new research job category is forming around formalizing aesthetic quality.
insights.quote: I have an $18.5 million seed round co- led by CRV and Amplify.

insights.claim: Taste Labs is going deep on visual design first and explicitly defers creative writing, sourcing supply instead through relationships with creative agencies and elite designers to license portfolio work that never shipped publicly.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: Unpublished agency portfolios are an unscraped, uncontaminated data supply — a licensing market that barely exists yet and could reprice agency archives.

insights.claim: Calacanis pitches an unexploited arbitrage: buying or exclusively licensing curated media archives such as Monocle or the fire-sale Paper magazine archive would cost a fraction of frontier-lab budgets while delivering decades of coalesced taste and the writers attached to it.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: A cheap-optionality trade on distressed legacy media IP if taste-training demand materializes; Taste Labs declined for now, leaving the asset class unbid.

themes.theme: The hollowed-out curator class as labor supply

insights.claim: Taste Labs' core input is a paid community of roughly 1,000 human 'tastemakers' recruited across deliberately distinct style buckets, media types, and specialties to preserve diversity rather than converge on one house aesthetic.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the human-in-the-loop cost base of subjective-domain data work and shows expert-network economics, not crowd labeling, are the model.
insights.quote: we have this awesome community of about like a thousand uh taste makers of different domains

insights.claim: Taste Labs is experimenting past hourly pay toward equity-like arrangements, full-time conversions, and letting tastemakers contribute their own portfolios into the company's design index in exchange for credit surfaced through its search-engine API rather than through hard model-output attribution.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: An early template for creator compensation in AI training that routes around the unsolved attribution problem — a model other data marketplaces may copy.
insights.quote: we're testing almost like allowing them to contribute their designs to our index

insights.claim: The professional critic class — film, restaurant, art reviewers of the newspaper and magazine era — has been gutted with no functional replacement, and the people who held those roles are currently struggling to find work.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris (co-host)
insights.so_what: Explains why high-quality taste labor is cheaply available right now — a temporary arbitrage for anyone building expert-curation businesses.
insights.quote: I don't feel like we have figured this out yet.

insights.claim: Taste is scarce because it requires enormous domain-specific exposure and trial and error, so no individual can hold it in more than a narrow area — the founder's own architect relatives have strong interior-design judgment and weak code judgment.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: Implies taste data must be assembled domain by domain, capping how fast any single vendor can expand and creating room for vertical specialists.
insights.quote: I think it's impossible for every human to develop taste in everything.

insights.claim: The founder rejects the assumption that AI destroys tastemakers, arguing mass production of mediocre output makes the extreme top of the quality distribution more valuable, not less.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: A barbell thesis for creative markets: bid the verifiable peak, short the undifferentiated middle — applies to agencies, designers, and premium media brands.
insights.quote: The more you have of this like mass production of things, the more I think the peak of the peak of the peak becomes valuable.

insights.claim: Calacanis built and runs a personal 'cool hunter' pipeline: a mega-prompt plus assistants that aggregate roughly 15 trusted curated sources including Monocle, run standing searches by city and category, and deliver a weekly trends report — a stack that surfaced a boutique Singapore hotel no mainstream search would return.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Demonstrates the working pattern today is trusted-source aggregation wrapped in an LLM, not model taste — the productizable gap Taste Labs and rivals are aiming at.

insights.claim: Calacanis plans to relaunch his annotated.com domain as an open marketplace where anyone can post rating and fact-checking tasks for consumers, explicitly to harvest and resell preference data to buyers like micro1.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: A named actor asserting preference data is the single most valuable data type right now — expect more consumer-facing preference-harvesting products.
insights.quote: nothing more valuable right now than preference data

insights.claim: The commoditization risk to taste is a half-life problem that predates AI: social media already compressed the cycle from avant-garde discovery to ubiquity, and the founder argues AI has not yet accelerated it only because model output is still too bad for real tastemakers to copy.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder)
insights.so_what: Frames a forward risk: once model output becomes good, trend cycles compress further and the durability of any taste-based brand shortens.

insights.claim: Japanese businesses are actively defending scarcity against discovery platforms — refusing tourists, switching menus and Google listings to Japanese only, and hiding signage — after TikTok and Instagram exposure overwhelmed places like Niseko and century-old noodle shops.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Evidence that supply-side gatekeeping is a real counter-strategy to algorithmic discovery, with implications for travel, hospitality, and local-listing platforms.

insights.claim: Leopold Aschenbrenner's AI-focused fund, founded 2024 by a 25-year-old ex-OpenAI researcher with no prior professional investing experience, grew from a few hundred million to over $45B AUM by July 2026 (the Wall Street Journal reported $20B in June) on a 439% net return through June 30th.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris (co-host)
insights.so_what: Sets the scale of the fastest AUM ramp in the AI trade and the size of the forced-selling overhang when it reversed.
insights.quote: he amassed over 45 billion in assets under management by July. In June, Wall Street Journal said 20 billion.

insights.claim: The fund's positions expressed the compute-demand thesis of the 2024 'Situational Awareness' paper through AI infrastructure and hardware names including SK Hynix, Micron, SanDisk, Bloom Energy, CoreWeave, and Nebius Group, with early backers including the Collison brothers, Daniel Gross, and Nat Friedman.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris (co-host)
insights.so_what: Names the exact basket that was liquidated — these tickers absorbed the forced supply and are where the pile-on pressure was concentrated.

insights.claim: The fund ran roughly 4x leverage, meaning a 25% drawdown in the underlying is a wipeout — Calacanis's benchmark for prudence is a margin loan against only 5-10% of a portfolio, which leaves room until one-to-one.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: A concrete rule of thumb for sizing margin against concentrated equity, and the explanation for why this blew up on a market that barely fell.
insights.quote: He was running according to the reports something like 4x leverage

insights.claim: Aschenbrenner described the unwind as a bank run: he was margin-called by his largest financing counterparties, and to raise cash sold the entire public portion of the portfolio to Ken Griffin's Citadel, so everything financed with borrowed money is gone.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris (co-host)
insights.so_what: Confirms the liquidation was counterparty-driven rather than a change of view, and that Citadel is now holding the AI-infra book at distressed entry prices.

insights.claim: The fund survives as a private-investment vehicle: private positions were not liquidated and include approximately $5B of Anthropic stock per the Financial Times, which is why Calacanis expects Aschenbrenner to come back stronger.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris (co-host) and Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: The public blowup does not imply distress in the private AI book — a ~$5B Anthropic stake is unimpaired and not a forced seller.

insights.claim: Aschenbrenner's LP letter, published by TBPN, took full responsibility and described vulnerability begetting more vulnerability, framing the decision to liquidate the public book as protecting LP capital while carrying on with the Anthropic shares.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris (co-host)
insights.so_what: Primary-source language on the failure mode; the reflexivity framing is the tell for how the position was risk-managed.
insights.quote: We came closer to permanent capital impairment than is acceptable to us.

insights.claim: Calacanis details the standard predation mechanic once a fund's positions and impending margin call are known: rivals holding the same names dump supply to force the price lower, then short to add pressure, while simultaneously negotiating to buy the distressed book.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: A reusable model for why crowded, levered positions gap far beyond fundamentals — watch for position-disclosure plus leverage as the setup.
insights.quote: Somebody starts falling, you just push them in the back.

insights.claim: Calacanis dismisses the conspiracy framing and explicitly separates this from FTX: Bankman-Fried's failure was fraud from commingling customer deposits with the trading fund, whereas Aschenbrenner's positions were legitimate bets destroyed by leverage.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Argues against reading this as systemic or criminal — no read-through to the industry's structural integrity, only to leverage discipline.
insights.quote: this is not an example of like something fundamentally wrong with the industry

insights.claim: The hosts read the intensity of the public pile-on as evidence of broad anti-AI sentiment finding a target rather than a market judgment, noting a slow news day, resentment of a young successful AI investor, and the fact that liquidation happened with the S&P only about 3% off its highs.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host) and Lon Harris (co-host)
insights.so_what: Sentiment marker: public hostility to AI wealth is now strong enough to shape narrative around AI-adjacent trades, a soft political risk for the sector.

insights.claim: Alphabet embedded its Nano Banana image generator directly into Google Earth, letting users reprompt satellite and street-view imagery — which was immediately used to fabricate a refugee camp at the US-Mexico border and a bomb crater beside a fake hospital in Gaza.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris (co-host)
insights.so_what: A live platform-liability event: closing the loop between authoritative imagery and generation is the specific design choice regulators and advertisers will target.

insights.claim: Calacanis's explanation for the Google Earth decision is organizational rather than strategic — a company-wide mandate to sprinkle AI onto every surface, with no owner asking whether the adjacency creates harm.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Predicts more self-inflicted trust incidents at large platforms racing to bolt on generation, and explains why Meta has not shipped the analogous Instagram feature.
insights.quote: everybody at that company is going hey AI is the next big thing sprinkle a little AI on everything

insights.claim: LinkedIn has reversed direction on generative AI, removing its 'let AI help you write your post' button and adding a 'report AI slop' button after users mass-produced low-effort AI posts.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris (co-host)
insights.so_what: First major platform to retract an AI writing feature on quality grounds — a template other feeds may follow, and a headwind for AI-writing tool distribution.
insights.quote: so many people were just hitting that button and lazily posting AI slap

insights.claim: Substack shipped a suite of anti-AI tools built by the company Pangram, and CEO Chris Best justified them by saying Substack must not turn into LinkedIn — flagging suspected AI posts at publish time and suggesting the writer make it sound more human.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris (co-host)
insights.so_what: AI-detection is becoming purchased platform infrastructure; Pangram is an early named vendor in a category with clear multi-platform demand.
insights.quote: We don't want Substack to turn into LinkedIn.

insights.claim: Calacanis argues detection must move from a publish-time nudge to distribution penalties — grey out or shadowban anything scoring above ~50-90% AI-generated and withhold homepage featuring — because warnings without ranking consequences will not change behavior.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: If ranking penalties become standard, AI-detection scores turn into a distribution tax — a direct business risk for AI content tooling and a moat for verified-human publishers.

insights.claim: Slop is already degrading core consumer feeds in ways users notice: fabricated shark-attack footage in Instagram recommendations and fake cartoon trains crowding out real train videos on YouTube for a child's search.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host) and Lon Harris (co-host)
insights.so_what: Concrete engagement-quality damage at Meta and YouTube — the mechanism by which slop becomes a measurable revenue problem rather than a discourse problem.

insights.claim: Calacanis reports his own teenage daughters refuse to use AI tools on principle, characterizing 10-to-15-year-olds' current view of AI as lame — a generational sentiment inversion relative to prior technology waves.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: If youth cohorts code AI as uncool, consumer AI faces a brand problem exactly where prior platforms found their earliest adopters.
insights.quote: AI is lame. Like that's what 10 to 15 year olds think right now.

themes.theme: Self-driving commoditization and the driver-jobs backlash

insights.claim: A single Stanford CS graduate, Ethan Goodart, built a working camera-and-vision-only self-driving golf cart with no lidar and is offering public rides around campus via a TestFlight app called Wind, with Sam Altman, Andrej Karpathy, and Jensen Huang among early beta riders.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris (co-host)
insights.so_what: Individual-scale autonomy demos are direct evidence the perception stack is commoditizing, which compresses the technical moat argument for AV valuations.

insights.claim: Calacanis claims his long-standing thesis that roughly 20 players reach self-driving at the same time is being validated, with Tesla furthest along on reliability nines, BYD launching, and Zoox receiving federal approval for 2,500 units with no steering wheel — while local approvals remain outstanding.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: If capability converges across ~20 entrants, the race resolves on scale, fleet operations, and licensing — favoring incumbents with distribution over pure technology bets.

insights.claim: Calacanis predicts drivers will be the first labor cohort visibly destroyed by AI — across ride-hailing and delivery at Uber and Uber Eats — with pay falling before jobs disappear, and discloses he holds investments in over 10 self-driving companies plus Uber, DoorDash, and Zipline.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Frames a wage-compression timeline in gig transport that precedes headcount loss — watch driver earnings data as the leading indicator, with disclosed positional bias.
insights.quote: the first wave of people losing their jobs to AI is going to be drivers

insights.claim: Calacanis argues China's suspension of new autonomous-vehicle permits, reported by Bloomberg as following a BYD outage, is actually about protecting driver employment rather than safety, and that this is a deliberate top-down freeze on fleet growth.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Reframes the largest AV market's regulatory risk as political-economic and therefore persistent — a durable ceiling on Chinese AV deployment forecasts.
insights.quote: China is freezing the number of self-driving cars on road. Why? It's not about safety. It's about protecting jobs,

insights.claim: Calacanis proposes that self-driving operators preemptively pay roughly $10,000 per vehicle per year into driver retraining and unemployment smoothing as the price of deployment approval, explicitly comparing it to Mark Cuban's suggestion that data centers pay locals off with free electricity.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: A concrete per-unit cost estimate for the political license to operate — worth modeling into AV and data-center unit economics as regulatory pressure builds.

themes.theme: Robotic solar buildout and the energy flywheel

insights.claim: Grit Robotics of San Francisco sells the AI layer, not the hardware, training off-the-shelf Kawasaki arms to unload, transport, and place utility-scale solar panels — with a human still required for the final fastening the robot cannot do precisely.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris (co-host)
insights.so_what: An asset-light robotics-software model attacking solar's labor-intensive installation cost, and a named specific company in the physical-AI buildout.

insights.claim: Calacanis argues the last human step in robotic solar installation is a design problem, not a dexterity problem — panels currently use bolt systems never designed for robot deployment, and a factory-installed clasp-and-hole mechanism would remove the human entirely.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Points at panel redesign for robotic assembly as the unlock for fully autonomous solar farms — a spec change that would advantage whichever manufacturer moves first.

insights.claim: Calacanis sketches a self-reinforcing desert buildout: place a panel factory in the middle of empty land, have robots place output radially outward, and let the driving distance grow to a few miles since robots do the transport — a fait accompli that scales without human labor or NIMBY opposition.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: A capex-light-per-marginal-watt geometry argument for why solar deployment could accelerate non-linearly once robotic placement works.

insights.claim: California recently hit 51% of energy from solar plus batteries, with comparable peaks in Germany on sunny days, continuous levels in Australia, and parts of South America — and on June 27th California roofed two irrigation canals with solar that both generates power and cut evaporation by 70%.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Canal-top solar is a dual-benefit siting model with almost no opposition surface — a specific deployment category to watch alongside grid-scale batteries.
insights.quote: California roof two irrigation canals with solar panels that makes electricity and cut the evaporation off the water lawn by 70%

insights.claim: Calacanis lays out a cascading resource thesis: solar plus batteries solves energy, solar-powered desalination then solves water, and cheap energy and water together solve agriculture, ending water-versus-electricity allocation fights.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: The bull case linking energy abundance to water and food — the framework behind investing in desal and agtech as downstream solar derivatives.

themes.theme: SF cost structure versus in-person density

insights.claim: A one-bedroom in San Francisco now averages $3,500-$4,600 per month, and hiring requires candidates to show up to apartment viewings with full documentation and prepaid funds, versus a roughly $2,000 outer-borough option reachable by subway in New York.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris (co-host) and Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Hard comp for modeling Bay Area salary premiums, and the structural reason SF-mandatory startups carry higher comp costs than distributed peers.
insights.quote: A onebedroom in San Francisco costs an average of 3500 to 4,600 per month right now.

insights.claim: Despite the housing cost, Taste Labs remains strictly in-person in San Francisco and relocated staff there, with the founder arguing the city's concentration of people produces something that cannot be reproduced elsewhere — while Austin's overbuilt inventory now yields three-months-free rent offers.
insights.speaker: Thais Castello Branco (Taste Labs founder) and Jason Calacanis (host)
insights.so_what: Frontier-adjacent AI startups are still paying the SF density premium deliberately — a signal that talent clustering, not cost, drives location choice in this cycle.
